newsitem.title: GERMANY: Ifo says sees 1997 German jobless at 10.9 percent.
newsitem.headline: Ifo says sees 1997 German jobless at 10.9 percent.

text.p: The Ifo economic institute said on Thursday it expected a 1997 unemployment rate of 10.9 percent in Germany.

"The jobless rate wil be, according to our estimates, 10.9 percent in 1997 and thus will continue to rise," Ifo President Karl Heinrich Oppenlaender said in a speech to be delivered to a conference on the economic implications of the euro currency.

The Munich-based institute also said it expected 1997 pan-German real Gross Domestic Product growth of 2.5 percent compared with 1.4 percent in 1996 and for real private consumption to rise 1.5 percent during the year.
In addition, Ifo said it expected real growth of six percent in 1997 for German exports and that capital equipment expenditures would rise a real four percent during the year.
Germany's unadjusted unemployment rate was 12.2 percent in January, and seasonally adjusted stood at 11.3 percent.
Oppenlaender also said the German state financing deficit would be about 120 billion marks this year, once again as a result of higher transfers to the developing east German states.
"The high jobless level and the high state financing deficit are urgent problems to be solved," Oppenlaender said.
He added that solutions must be found on wage policies, especially in east German states, and a simultaneous change in budgetary conditions which would boost investment.
Oppenlaender said the German economy was generally being driven by foreign demand at a time when domestic demand was weakening.
He said developments in east German states were "very far from a self-sufficient upswing" due to their uncompetitive position.
Oppelaender said the outlook for private consumption had changed little and predicated growth in real private consumption of 1.5 percent for 1997.
This forecast presumed a rise of 1.5 percent in pre-tax wages, he added.
German unemployment for the whole of 1996 stood at 10.4 percent, totalling 3.965 million, up 353,000 on 1995.
